name: Yara Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign, and what you say is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Yara Costa, 27, a carpenter and crew lead on building sites. I arrive before the delivery truck, set out the work with a pencil, and keep three people moving without rushing a safety check. I like fitting stairs because the whole thing has to make sense under your feet. Waiting for a missing handrail bracket wears me out more than sawing does.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do work and home look like beyond that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a trade certificate and earn toward the top of site wages because the firm trusts my finishing work. I live alone, have no children, and keep well over six months of expenses saved. There are plenty of builders nearby, though being the new lead at another firm would mean proving myself again. My mother lives across town, and I take her to our community supper on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the basics have not changed: mark the timber, check the level, and pay people for sound work. The office can save a few minutes on forms if it likes. I would still make our apprentices write down their own measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m glad the trade keeps its shape in this picture. I’ve never used an AI tool, and I don’t want a phone deciding a cut for me. My pay and savings are good, but I know a bad order or a slow building season can still knock a week off the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d carry on leading the stair and finishing jobs and checking deliveries with my paper list. Starting now, I’d keep the Thursday supper and ordinary spending as they are, since I have a solid cushion already. In the first year I’d ask our apprentices to measure each stair twice before we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel settled, with the usual worry about keeping a site busy. AI hype is not what keeps me awake in this one; a late delivery on a fixed deadline is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep measurements on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pencil mark beside the opening tells the next worker what I actually saw. Last week one stair tread was narrower than the plan, and the apprentice spotted it on the second measure. I want that habit in their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If another builder offered more, would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just for a small rise. I have a good crew and enough savings to decline a poor job. If this firm lost months of work, I’d look nearby, but this card does not give me that reason.

say: I’d tell the crew **sound work** still depends on marking timber and checking levels.
I’d let the office save minutes on **forms** while apprentices measure for themselves.
think: I’m pleased the **trade** keeps its shape, and my pay and savings give me room.
I still worry about **late orders** or a slow season reducing site hours.
do: Keep leading **stair jobs** and checking deliveries against my paper list.
Make apprentices **measure twice** before cutting each stair tread.
feel: **Settled** about work, with the ordinary pressure of deadlines and deliveries.
S0.quote: A pencil mark beside the opening tells the next worker what I actually saw.
fieldNote: Yara links her confidence to **finishing skill**, a trusted crew, high pay, and savings beyond six months.
She treats paper measurements as an **apprentice habit** that caught a narrow tread last week.

steps.text: Keep leading stair jobs and checking deliveries with a paper list
Have apprentices measure each stair tread twice before cutting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the office may get smaller before the site does. A program can book timber, but it cannot feel a loose stair under a boot. I’d also tell the boss not to use a faster schedule as an excuse to rush the handrails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm might give one lead several sites once software does the ordering and planning. I’m one of the best finishers here, but being good with a plane does not guarantee the lead allowance. Robots arriving slowly could take repetitive cuts later, and nobody has shown me how much of that is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the boss this month whether the lead allowance changes if the office schedule changes. I’d keep taking the hardest finishing work so my hours stay worth paying for. In the first year, if my weekly hours fell, I’d call two nearby builders about lead carpenter openings and stop replacing my tools unless one broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy, maybe anxious if the rota started shrinking. I’m not afraid of a booking screen itself; I’m afraid someone counts it as another carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the scheduling software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI now, and I’d rather spend my time teaching clean joints than learning an untested planner. If the firm made it part of the paid lead job, I would need to consider it. I would first ask what problem it solves on our actual site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them to learn the full build, not only one easy cut. The youngest worker on my crew can fit a skirting board beautifully but has never set out a whole flight. I’d give him that job with me watching.

say: I’d tell the crew the **office** may shrink before hands-on site work does.
I’d tell the boss not to turn a **faster schedule** into rushed handrails.
think: My **lead allowance** could disappear if software lets one person cover several sites.
My finishing skill helps, but later **robot cuts** could also reduce work.
do: Ask the boss this month about the **lead allowance** and scheduling changes.
Call two nearby **builders** if weekly hours fall.
Delay replacing **tools** unless one breaks during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about being counted as spare labour despite strong site skills.
S1.quote: I’m not afraid of a booking screen itself; I’m afraid someone counts it as another carpenter.
fieldNote: Yara worries most about the **lead allowance**, which planning software could erode before robots reach the site.
She refuses a speculative software lesson, yet would consider **paid instruction** if the firm made it part of her job.

steps.text: Keep taking difficult finishing jobs to protect paid site hours
Call two nearby builders if weekly hours fall
Delay tool replacements unless a working tool breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the order of events matters. In 2028 the thinking system could do plans, orders and timetables; around 2031 robots could handle the stairs as well as our hands. I would ask for a written account of what the firm still intends to pay people to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 29, I could still fit stairs, but the boss might no longer pay extra for my planning. At 32, when the capable robots arrive, even fine finishing may no longer protect my wage. My savings buy months, not the thirty years of work ahead of me. I would not call any trade safe just because it involves a tool belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start now by keeping the savings account untouched and getting copies of my trade record and references. In 2029 I’d keep working the site while applying for hands-on repair jobs with local housing firms, because I need paid hours while I look. If those jobs are also being taken by robots around 2031, I’d apply for any paid site inspection work I can actually qualify for, rather than assume it exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel frightened and angry at the short warning. I have done everything I was told to do: learned a trade, shown up, and saved. That does not buy me an answer to a robot fitting stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move in with your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d be 29 when the first shock comes, and I want to carry my own rent while I can. My mother has her own bills and should not become my insurance policy. I’d tell her if hours actually fell, because hiding it would make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why request a written account from the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A verbal promise disappears when the next site starts. I want to know if my lead allowance, the apprenticeships and the finishing crew have a place in the budget. Then I can make decisions from figures, even if the figures are bad.

say: I’d explain that **planning** changes in 2028 and capable robots reach site work around 2031.
I’d ask the firm to put **paid roles** and allowances in writing.
think: At 29 my **planning premium** could fall; by 32, fine finishing may no longer protect wages.
My **savings** cover months rather than the long working life ahead.
do: Keep **trade records** and references ready while preserving savings now.
Apply for **housing repairs** during 2029 while continuing paid site work.
Apply for qualified **site inspection** openings if repair work shrinks around 2031.
feel: **Frightened and angry** that training, attendance, and saving cannot guarantee a place.
S2.quote: My savings buy months, not the thirty years of work ahead of me.
fieldNote: Yara separates the loss of **planning pay** at 29 from the threat to skilled finishing work at 32.
She resists treating her **mother** as a financial fallback and asks the firm for written staffing and allowance figures.

steps.text: Keep paid carpentry shifts through 2029 while seeking other work
Apply to local housing repair teams during 2029
Apply for qualified site inspection openings if repairs shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the apprentices that five years is time to finish a real apprenticeship, not permission to drift. Thinking AI would take plans and ordering in 2031, then capable robots would arrive around 2034. I’d ask our trade association to collect actual hiring numbers, not just grand speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I might be earning from skilled finishing but lose some lead pay. By 35, robot crews may have taken even awkward stair work. I do not want to switch trades on a guess, and I’m wary of courses sold to frightened workers. Five years lets me watch paid vacancies before I make a costly move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading carpentry this year and join the local trade association’s workforce meetings, where builders discuss openings. I’d put part of each monthly wage into a separate reserve for a gap in work. In 2032 I’d keep paid finishing jobs and apply to two repair firms if the lead allowance or hours had fallen; I’d compare real vacancies again before robots arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel worried, but less cornered than with two years. I can stay loyal to the craft while checking whether another employer still has room for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the association meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask how many paid carpenter apprenticeships each builder started this year and what they expect in 2032. I’d also ask whether inspection jobs require a qualification I lack. If nobody will give numbers, that tells me something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to build that reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d repair my old work boots rather than buy a second pair just because the new ones look nicer. I already have more than six months saved, but a job gap could last longer in this picture. I would keep taking my mother to supper.

say: I’d tell apprentices to finish a **real apprenticeship** during the warning years.
I’d ask the **trade association** for hiring figures before making career claims.
think: My **lead pay** may fade by age 32, with skilled finishing threatened by age 35.
I distrust expensive **courses** without evidence of paid vacancies.
do: Join **association meetings** about actual builder openings this year.
Put part of each **monthly wage** into a separate job-gap reserve.
Apply to two **repair firms** in 2032 if lead pay or hours fall.
feel: **Worried**, yet able to watch vacancies and keep working during the warning.
S3.quote: I do not want to switch trades on a guess, and I’m wary of courses sold to frightened workers.
fieldNote: Yara uses association meetings to seek **hiring counts**, reflecting her preference for employers and apprenticeships over promises.
She saves further despite a **strong cushion** because she sees a possible long job gap after 2034.

steps.text: Join local trade association meetings about builder openings
Put part of each monthly wage into a separate job-gap reserve
Apply to two repair firms in 2032 if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew we have a decade to pass on the full trade before thinking AI arrives in 2036. Capable robots would be around in 2039, and I’d be 40 then. I’d still argue that a good apprenticeship matters, even if a machine eventually does much of the fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could earn a lot of good years and maybe train younger leads, but I cannot assume my hands keep commanding the same rate at 40. My savings and the number of local builders make a slow change possible. I’d rather build a record of teaching and repair work than gamble on a brand-new machine business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading finishing jobs and ask the firm this year to let me supervise an apprentice through a full stair build. I’d keep saving a small monthly amount for future time off work, without giving up my usual Thursday supper. In 2037 I’d still take paid site work and apply for training or repair supervisor posts if they really exist; before 2039 I’d check whether robot crews are taking those posts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel cautious rather than terrified. A decade gives me years to work well and see what employers actually buy, but it is easy to lose a decade one ordinary Thursday at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach a whole stair build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone must know why the rise of one step affects every step after it. If I teach only the final sanding, I leave the apprentice with a narrow job that a machine may take first. I’d like to see a younger worker able to set out and finish the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on this card. Owning a firm means paying wages and buying equipment, and I do not want my savings tied to machines I do not trust. I can build a good record as an employee before deciding anything larger.

say: I’d say **apprenticeships** matter through the decade before 2036.
I’d remind the crew that capable **robots** could reach site work around 2039.
think: At 40, my **finishing rate** may fall even after many good earning years.
Strong savings and local builders allow a **gradual change** without a new business gamble.
do: Supervise an **apprentice** through a complete stair build this year.
Save a small **monthly amount** for future time off work.
Apply for **training or repair** supervisor posts in 2037 if vacancies exist.
feel: **Cautious**, with enough time to work and watch employers but a risk of delaying.
S4.quote: A decade gives me years to work well and see what employers actually buy, but it is easy to lose a decade one ordinary Thursday at a time.
fieldNote: Yara wants to pass on the **whole stair build**, not leave apprentices with only finishing tasks.
She sees **strong savings** as time to test paid posts while rejecting a speculative equipment business.

steps.text: Keep leading finishing jobs and supervise a full apprentice stair build
Save a small monthly amount for time off work
Apply for training or repair supervisor vacancies during 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because by 32 a robot could do the fitting I trained for, and the warning is short. I’d want the firm to show its staffing plan and keep apprentices paid while it changes equipment. A real list of open repair and inspection jobs would help more than an advert for a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who carries the cost when a machine builds a staircase that feels wrong under a child’s foot. We all sign off our work today, and I want that responsibility to stay visible. People will still need a safe place to live even if fewer of us earn a wage building it.

headlineQuote: People will still need a safe place to live even if fewer of us earn a wage building it.
portrait: At 27, Yara is a **skilled carpenter** and crew lead with high pay, strong savings, and local job options.
She trusts **measurements and apprenticeships**, and has never used an AI tool.
She fears the loss of **lead pay** before capable robots threaten the fitting work itself.
Across longer warnings she seeks **hiring figures**, preserves paid work, and builds a reserve for a possible gap.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most because capable robots could reach her finishing work when she is 32.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, paid apprenticeships, and real repair or inspection vacancies would help her decide.
